title: What triggers an R&D tax credit audit?
description: Claiming the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41 does not automatically trigger an IRS audit.

body.text: Claiming the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41 does not automatically trigger an IRS audit. For U.S. businesses, audits typically stem from DIF scoring, random National Research Program sampling, and red flags such as disproportionately large credits, unexplained QRE spikes, amended-return refund claims (which the IRS screens 100%), industry code mismatches, and excluded activities.

Claiming the federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit—formally titled the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41)—does not automatically trigger an Internal Revenue Service (IRS) examination. Rather, R&D tax credit audits are initiated through a combination of algorithmic statistical screening—primarily the IRS's Discriminant Function (DIF) scoring system for small and mid-market returns and mandatory classification routing for large corporate returns—random compliance sampling under the National Research Program (NRP), and targeted administrative reviews of high-risk filing behaviors. Across these institutional selection pathways, examinations are overwhelmingly triggered by quantitative anomalies (credits that are disproportionately large relative to gross receipts, payroll, or established industry norms, or unexplained year-over-year spikes in Qualified Research Expenses [QREs]), high-scrutiny procedural actions (most notably claiming R&D refunds on amended tax returns, which undergo 100% IRS validity screening), incompatible industry classification codes, and cascading red flags originating in other sections of a federal income tax return.

Once a tax return is flagged by automated screening or selected for review, the legal sustainability of the claimed credit depends on satisfying two distinct legal thresholds: upfront procedural specificity under Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1) (26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1)) and substantive project-to-expense nexus under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d)).

Maloy formally abolished the Tiered Issue Process on August 17, 2012, withdrawing all Tier I Industry Director Directives and replacing them with domestic Issue Practice Groups (IPGs) and International Practice Networks (IPNs).

United States: While the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California dismissed the taxpayers' refund suit for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under 26 U.S.C. § 7422(a) and 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) on April 25, 2019, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded that dismissal on February 25, 2021 (Harper v. United States, 847 Fed. App'x 408), holding that the IRS waived its specificity objection by conducting a four-year substantive audit and denying the claim on the merits. Simultaneously, the redesigned Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) introduces Section G (Business Component Information), which is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 and mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 for taxpayers not meeting statutory small-business exemptions.

body.text: The Regulatory Environment and Mechanics of R&D Audit Initiation

A persistent misconception among business owners, tax directors, and financial executives is that submitting Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) automatically triggers an IRS audit. According to official IRS examination guidance (updated February 17, 2026), claiming a tax credit or receiving a tax refund does not automatically initiate an examination. Nevertheless, because the R&D tax credit involves complex technical, scientific, and cost-accounting determinations under I.R.C. § 41, claiming the incentive places the tax return within a specialized compliance framework where statistical anomalies, aggressive allocations, and documentation gaps receive heightened administrative scrutiny.
Algorithmic Screening (DIF) and Random Selection (NRP)

The IRS conducts annual compliance examinations across all entity types—individuals, corporations, S corporations, partnerships, and fiduciaries—using a combination of statistical screening models and random compliance selection. Under Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) 4.1.2 (Workload Identification, Selection and Delivery, updated April 30, 2026) and IRM 4.22.1 (National Research Program (NRP), updated April 30, 2026), these selection mechanisms operate through four distinct institutional channels.

First, the IRS evaluates tax returns using confidential mathematical formulas known as the Discriminant Function (DIF) system, which assigns a numeric DIF score measuring the probability of significant tax adjustment upon audit. Under IRM 4.1.2, DIF mathematical formulas are strictly confidential and for official use only, and a return's assigned DIF score may not be disclosed. Generally, the higher the DIF score assigned to a return, the greater its audit potential, and Field Case Selection (FCS) analysts establish annual national DIF cutoff scores by activity code to order the highest-scored returns for examination. Returns computer-scored under the DIF system encompass Individual, Corporation, S Corporation, Partnership, and Fiduciary filings. For corporate filers (Form 1120), returns having no balance sheet or total assets under $10,000,000 are computer-scored under the corporate DIF system across five specific asset strata:

items: Activity Code 203: No Balance Sheet.
Activity Code 209: Assets under $250,000.
Activity Code 213: Assets of $250,000 to under $1,000,000.
Activity Code 215: Assets of $1,000,000 to under $5,000,000.
Activity Code 217: Assets of $5,000,000 to under $10,000,000.

body.text: Second, high-asset corporate returns reporting total assets of $10,000,000 or more—designated under IRM 4.1.2 as Activity Codes 219 through 230—are not computer-scored under the DIF system. Instead, IRM 4.1.2 mandates that these returns are delivered automatically to classification at the Large Business and International (LB&I) Campus in Ogden, Utah. Certain miscellaneous corporate returns—specifically Forms 1120-L, 1120-PC, 1120-H, 1120-SF, 1120-REIT, 1120-RIC, and 1120-ND—are also not DIF-scored, though they may be sample-ordered and screened at the receiving campus prior to shipment to Statistics of Income (SOI) at the Ogden Campus, while specialized corporate returns designated as "Specials" are ordered via specific audit codes under IRM 3.11.16.9.1.

Third, beginning historically with the Audit Control Program in 1948 and the Taxpayer Compliance Measurement Program (TCMP, 1962–1988), and operating since 2001 under the National Research Program (NRP) overseen by Research, Applied Analytics, and Statistics (RAAS) following the IRS Restructuring and Reform Act of 1998 (RRA '98), the IRS selects a statistically valid random sample of returns each year to measure filing, payment, and reporting compliance. Unlike earlier line-by-line compliance audits, NRP examinations rely on pre-contact case building—analyzing internal IRS Master Files, the Compliance Data Warehouse (CDW), and publicly available data to rule out compliance issues before contacting the taxpayer. Data collected from NRP examinations capture both misreported and accurately reported line items across the filing population to estimate the federal tax gap and continuously recalibrate the statistical "norms" and DIF workload selection formulas, shielding compliant taxpayers from unnecessary audits while increasing selection precision for non-compliant returns.

Fourth, the IRS selects returns through related-party and preparer-network examinations. Under IRS examination procedures, a return may be selected when it involves issues, transactions, or flow-through items connected to other taxpayers—such as business partners, S corporation shareholders, investors, or related corporate entities—whose returns have already been selected for examination, or where operational selection models detect systemic noncompliance patterns across a shared tax preparer or R&D advisory network.
Historical Evolution: From the 2007 Tier I Directive to Modern Gatekeeping

On April 4, 2007, the IRS Large and Mid-Size Business Division (LMSB) issued Industry Director Directive #1 on Research Credit Claims, followed by Tier I Research Credit Claims Issue Directive #2 (Control No. LMSB-4-0608-035, effective September 4, 2007, when Lavena B. Williams, Director, Field Operations-East, was appointed Issue Owner Executive, and formally issued on January 15, 2009 by Patricia C. Chaback, Industry Director for Communications, Technology & Media) and the May 2008 Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG): Credit for Increasing Research Activities § 41 (LMSB-04-0508-030). These directives designated Research Credit Refund Claims ("RC Claims"—defined as claims for credit or refund of an overpayment of tax generated in whole or in part by the research credit and not taken into account on an original return) as a Tier I compliance issue of high strategic importance across all LMSB industries. Under LMSB-4-0608-035, examiners were required to track RC Claims using ERCS Project/Tracking Code 0551 (and IMS Version 3.0 SAIN Code 605, UIL Code 41.00–41.56, and Issue Tracking Attribute Code C160) and to issue a Mandatory Research Credit Claim Information Document Request (Mandatory IDR, Exhibit C of the RCCATG) on all selected RC Claims (and all claims under examination prior to the audit mid-point) to combat prepackaged, marketed studies relying on high-level estimates, invalid assumptions, and contingency fee arrangements. Concurrently, on May 25, 2007, Congress enacted the U.S. Troop Readiness, Veterans' Care, Katrina Recovery, and Iraq Accountability Appropriations Act of 2007, adding I.R.C. § 6676(a), which imposes a 20% penalty on the disallowed "excessive amount" of any erroneous claim for refund or credit that lacks a reasonable basis.

On August 17, 2012, however, LB&I Commissioner Heather C. Maloy issued a formal directive immediately ending the Tiered Issue Process across all Tier I, Tier II, and Tier III issues—including the Tier I classification of the R&D tax credit—after an internal review concluded that the tiering structure (originally introduced in 2006 to combat abusive tax shelters and listed transactions) was ill-suited for ongoing corporate compliance management. Commissioner Maloy's August 17, 2012 directive formally withdrew all prior Industry Director Directives (IDDs) relevant to tiered issues, rendered IRM and Coordinated Issue Paper references to tiered status invalid, and replaced Tier I oversight with a collaborative knowledge management network of domestic Issue Practice Groups (IPGs) and International Practice Networks (IPNs). While the substantive examination techniques of the May 2008 RCCATG remain foundational to examiner training and risk assessment, R&D tax credit claims are no longer audited under the 2007 Tier I directive. Instead, following major 2009 judicial decisions that tempered overly restrictive IRS interpretations (such as Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, and United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009)) and a subsequent wave of 2021–2026 appellate and Tax Court substantiation and funded-research rulings (Little Sandy Coal, Moore, Harper, Grigsby, Smith), modern IRS enforcement focuses on upfront administrative validity screening under Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F and itemized business-component disclosures on the redesigned Form 6765.
Contemporary IRS Enforcement Resources: Correcting the "87,000 Agents" Narrative

First, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 did not mandate the hiring of 87,000 revenue agents (auditors). Rather, the figure originated in a May 2021 U.S. Department of the Treasury report, The American Families Plan Tax Compliance Agenda, which projected that an approximately $80 billion ($79,167 million) ten-year mandatory and discretionary cap-adjustment investment would allow the IRS to incrementally add a cumulative 86,852 full-time equivalent (FTE) positions by Year 10 (FY2031)—growing from 5,197 FTEs in Year 1 to 86,852 FTEs in Year 10—across all agency functions. That projection encompassed taxpayer customer service, information technology modernization (allocating nearly $6 billion to replace 1960s-era master files, integrate over 60 legacy case management systems, and deploy machine-learning audit selection analytics), cybersecurity defenses, operations support, and routine retirement/attrition replacement, alongside a targeted $6.7 billion Program Integrity Allocation to hire and retain at least 5,000 specialized enforcement personnel focused on high-income individuals, complex partnerships, multi-tier pass-through entities, and large multinational corporations.

Second, according to IRS Publication 5316 (Rev. 1-2026), the projected 86,852 FTE expansion never materialized in full. After reaching a staffing baseline of just over 96,000 FTEs in FY2024 (still below the agency's 1995 staffing level of over 112,000 FTEs), the IRS experienced legislative funding rescissions, budget cuts, mandatory dismissals of probationary hires, and Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) workforce reduction initiatives—including Voluntary Early Retirement Authority (VERA), Reductions in Force (RIFs), and deferred resignation programs—resulting in the loss of more than 25% of the IRS's overall workforce. As a critical second-order implication for R&D tax credit claimants, because the IRS's human examination workforce contracted by over 25% rather than doubling, the agency relies even more heavily on automated algorithmic filters, machine-learning anomaly detection, mandatory upfront Form 6765 Section G data fields, and summary campus rejection of procedurally deficient refund claims before ever assigning a field revenue agent.
Substantiation, Procedural Specificity, and the Risk and Rights Framework

The primary vulnerability for an R&D tax credit claimant is not merely the initiation of an examination, but the legal and evidentiary sustainability of the claim once selected for review. Sustaining an R&D claim requires satisfying three interlocking legal frameworks: substantive recordkeeping and project-to-expense nexus under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d); procedural specificity for refund claims under 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1); and contractual financial risk and substantial rights requirements under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d), and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e).
Recordkeeping Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d) and the Project-to-Expense Nexus

Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) (26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d), promulgated in Treasury Decision 9104, 69 FR 22, January 2, 2004, effective for taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2003), the recordkeeping requirement for the research credit states verbatim:

"A taxpayer claiming a credit under section 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. For the rules governing record retention, see § 1.6001-1."

When the Treasury Department and the IRS issued T.D. 9104 in January 2004 (accompanied by Notice 2004-11 establishing the research credit recordkeeping agreement pilot program), they eliminated an earlier pre-2001 regulatory requirement that mandated a rigid, predefined list of contemporaneous documents, replacing it with the flexible "sufficiently usable form and detail" standard cross-referencing general tax recordkeeping under I.R.C. § 6001 and 26 C.F.R. § 1.6001-1. However, both the IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG, LMSB-04-0508-030) and recent federal appellate and Tax Court decisions demonstrate that flexibility in record format does not relax the taxpayer's substantive burden of proof. As the Fifth Circuit emphasized in United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672, 675 (5th Cir. 2009), tax credits are a matter of legislative grace, are allowed only as clearly provided for by statute, and must be substantiated by the taxpayer bearing the burden of proof.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A), the four-part qualification test must be applied separately with respect to each discrete business component of the taxpayer—defined under § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. The IRS RCCATG defines the inability to connect specific research projects and underlying qualified research activities (QRAs) to the specific qualified research expenses (QREs—wages, supplies, and contract research costs) claimed at the business-component level as the "nexus problem". As the RCCATG explains, while a project-based accounting system captures research costs directly at the discrete business-component level and thereby establishes the required nexus between qualified activities and claimed expenditures, cost-center accounting captures expenditures by organizational department for financial or operational reporting without regard to whether the underlying activities satisfy I.R.C. § 41 statutory criteria. In practice, many disallowed claims rely on hybrid methodologies that capture total Form W-2 wages in a cost center and multiply them by an arbitrary overall percentage based on uncorroborated manager or Subject Matter Expert (SME) recollections rather than measurable, corroborative project records. Under the RCCATG and Form 6765 instructions, taxpayers must substantiate 100% of the claimed credit across all business components unless they utilize a valid statistical sample conforming to Revenue Procedure 2011-42; non-statistical "judgment sampling" and uncorroborated estimates under I.R.C. § 6001 are rejected as non-auditable.

Recent judicial decisions reinforce this strict substantiation burden across both project activities and employee compensation. First, with respect to the 80% "substantially all" activity fraction, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(6) dictate that "substantially all" of a taxpayer's research activities with respect to a business component—defined as 80% or more of a taxpayer's research activities measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and without regard to § 1.41-2(d)(2))—must constitute elements of a process of experimentation that relates to a qualified purpose under § 41(d)(3). In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), the U.S. Tax Court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit disallowed 100% of a shipbuilder's claimed research credits for designing and constructing a tank barge and a dry dock. Although the Seventh Circuit rejected categorical reasoning that would automatically exclude pilot-model construction from experimentation—clarifying that building a pilot model can be part of a process of experimentation when it aids in evaluating alternatives and resolving technical uncertainty—it held that merely labeling a completed vessel a "prototype" is insufficient. The taxpayer failed because it lacked records quantifying the regulatory experimental-activity fraction, where the numerator is research activities constituting elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, and the denominator is total research activities with respect to the component falling within § 174 and not excluded by § 41(d)(4) (with supply costs excluded from the activity fraction because supplies are not "activities"). As the Seventh Circuit admonished, I.R.C. § 41(d) requires courts to "walk by sight, not by faith".

Second, with respect to executive wage allocations and the "one-up" direct supervision rule, in Scott Moore and Gayla Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20 (affirmed by the Seventh Circuit in 2024), the taxpayers owned Nevco, Inc., an S corporation manufacturing athletic scoreboards, video displays, and sports-venue technology across projects including the Scoreboard Truss, Scorbitz cloud platform, New Caney Ribbon Board, MPCX-2 wireless controller, and Slim Shot Clock. While the IRS conceded the QRE eligibility of wages paid to Nevco's staff engineers and their immediate supervisor (Director of Engineering Dave Paslay), the Tax Court disallowed 100% of the taxpayers' claimed 65% allocation of the salary and bonuses of Nevco's President and Chief Operating Officer (Gary Robert) for tax years 2014 and 2015. The court established three critical audit principles: time spent on broad "new product development" (which includes market research, aesthetic design, budgeting, staffing, and customer feedback) is not synonymous with statutory "qualified research"; standard payroll logs showing total hours worked without task-specific tracking do not satisfy 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d); and under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(c)(2), "direct supervision" means the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research and explicitly "does not include supervision by a higher-level manager to whom first-line managers report, even if that manager is a qualified research scientist". Because the COO supervised the Director of Engineering rather than the hands-on engineers, he was two layers removed from the research ("supervision of supervision"). Furthermore, consistent with Eustace v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-66, aff'd, 312 F.3d 1254 (7th Cir. 2002), and Shami v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2012-78, both the Tax Court and the Seventh Circuit refused to estimate qualified time under the Cohan rule (Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)) because the taxpayers lacked a credible evidentiary baseline to quantify the fraction of executive hours dedicated to experimentation.
Procedural Specificity Under 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) and the Harper Litigation

First, the quoted specificity requirement does not appear in the text of Form 6765; rather, it is the formal administrative exhaustion rule of Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1) (26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1)), which governs all tax refund or credit claims and serves as a mandatory jurisdictional prerequisite to filing a federal tax refund lawsuit under 26 U.S.C. § 7422(a) (United States v. Memphis Cotton Oil Co.; Stoller v. United States; Boyd v. United States, 762 F.2d 1369 (9th Cir. 1985); Synergy Staffing, Inc. v. United States, 323 F.3d 1157 (9th Cir. 2003)). Under the verbatim text of 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1):

"(1) No refund or credit will be allowed after the expiration of the statutory period of limitation applicable to the filing of a claim therefor except upon one or more of the grounds set forth in a claim filed before the expiration of such period. The claim must set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis thereof. The statement of the grounds and facts must be verified by a written declaration that it is made under the penalties of perjury. A claim which does not comply with this paragraph will not be considered for any purpose as a claim for refund or credit."

As explained in Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F (citing Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, Computervision Corp. v. United States, and IA 80 Group, Inc. & Subsidiaries v. United States), the regulation distinguishes between the legal ground for a claim and the specific underlying facts supporting it. Once the IRS rejects a facially deficient refund claim on procedural grounds, that claim is disposed of and cannot be amended or perfected as a matter of right after the statutory period of limitations has expired (Tobin v. Tomlinson; PALA, Inc.; Newport Industries v. United States).

Second, in Harper v. United States, No. 3:18-cv-02110-DMS-LL, 2019 WL 1877185 (S.D. Cal. Apr. 25, 2019), appellants Jeffrey A. Harper and Katherine M. Harper (sole shareholders of Subchapter S corporation Harper Construction Company ["HCC"]) filed amended returns (Forms 1040X and 1120X attaching Forms 6765) claiming I.R.C. § 41 research credits of $437,632 for tax year 2008 and $388,325 for tax year 2010. Following an intensive four-year substantive audit in which the IRS issued detailed questionnaires regarding HCC's project accounting, business components, the § 41(d)(1)(C) "substantially all" rule, and employee salary breakdowns—and the taxpayers produced over 100,000 pages of supporting documentation (over 112,000 pages per the appellate concurrence)—the IRS issued a final determination denying the claim on the merits ("You have not shown you are entitled to the claimed refund"). When the Harpers filed a refund suit in the Southern District of California, the government moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under 26 U.S.C. § 7422(a), arguing that the initial Forms 6765 presented only numerical calculations without identifying specific business components, employee activities, or four-part test facts under 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1).

Although District Judge Dana M. Sabraw granted the government's motion to dismiss in April 2019, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded on February 25, 2021 in Jeffrey A. Harper; Katherine M. Harper v. United States of America, No. 19-55933, 847 Fed. App'x 408, 2021 WL 732970 (9th Cir. Feb. 25, 2021) (before Circuit Judges Linn, Rawlinson, and Hunsaker). Applying the Supreme Court's waiver doctrine under Angelus Milling Co. v. Commissioner, 325 U.S. 293 (1945), the Ninth Circuit majority held that the IRS unmistakably waived enforcement of its regulatory specificity requirement under 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) by conducting a targeted four-year substantive examination and rendering a final determination on the merits without ever objecting to form or specificity defects. Circuit Judge Hunsaker concurred in the judgment, reasoning that because the taxpayers did not brief waiver below, jurisdiction was properly established under the informal claim doctrine of United States v. Kales, 314 U.S. 186 (1941), as the initial Forms 6765 provided written notice that was perfected during the audit by submitting over 112,000 pages of documentation.

Third, because the Ninth Circuit held in Harper that auditing a vague R&D refund claim on the merits waives the IRS's specificity defense under 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1), the IRS Office of Chief Counsel issued Chief Counsel Memorandum (CCM) 20214101F on October 15, 2021 (accompanied by IRS News Release IR-2021-203). CCM 20214101F explicitly analyzed the district and appellate rulings in Harper and instructed IRS campus personnel to screen all amended R&D refund claims at intake before initiating an examination—rejecting facially deficient claims out of hand as non-processible so that no substantive audit waiver can occur. Similarly, in Premier Tech, Inc. v. United States, No. 2:20-cv-890 (D. Utah July 15, 2022), the government moved to dismiss an amended R&D refund suit under 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) for failing to itemize projects, components, and project-tied wages/supplies on the face of the filing; although the district court ruled in favor of Premier Tech because historic Form 6765 did not explicitly request those fields, the litigation directly catalyzed the IRS's upfront amended-return rules and the addition of Section G to Form 6765.
Contractual Eligibility: The Financial Risk and Substantial Rights Tests

Technical eligibility in an R&D audit extends beyond scientific experimentation into legal and financial contract analysis under the "risk and rights tests". Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), statutory qualified research expressly excludes "funded research"—defined as "Any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)". As the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit explained in United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023) (citing Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995)), two "mirror image" Treasury Regulations—26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d) for the research performer and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e) for the customer/payor—allocate the research tax credit to whichever party bears the financial risk of failure and holds substantial rights to the research results.

When a taxpayer performs research for a customer or client under contract, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(2) evaluates all agreements (not merely formal research contracts) entered into between the performing taxpayer and third parties on an item-by-item, contract-by-contract basis, treating the research as "funded" (and therefore ineligible for the credit by the performer) unless the performer satisfies both the financial risk prong and the substantial rights prong. Under the financial risk / contingency of payment prong of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), "Amounts payable under any agreement that are contingent on the success of the research and thus considered to be paid for the product or result of the research (see § 1.41-2(e)(2)) are not treated as funding". Fixed-price contracts where payment is contingent on delivering a successful technical result meeting detailed specifications (as in Fairchild Industries, where the contract contained 1,000 pages of detailed technical specifications requiring formal customer acceptance before payment) and where the contractor absorbs cost overruns generally satisfy the financial risk standard. Conversely, cost-plus, time-and-materials, or milestone-approval contracts lacking strict technical-success contingencies where the performer is paid for its work regardless of technical success are treated as funded to the extent of the payments received (and under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A, Example 1, a wholly compensated researcher is barred from the credit regardless of any rights retained).

Under the substantial rights prong of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), if a taxpayer performing research for another person "retains no substantial rights in research under the agreement providing for the research," the research is treated as fully funded and no credit is allowed. In Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50, partners in the architectural firm AS+GG challenged the validity of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d) following the Supreme Court's overruling of Chevron deference in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. 369 (2024); the Tax Court rejected the challenge and upheld § 1.41-4A(d) based on Skidmore deference (citing its longevity and clarity) and pre-Loper Bright Federal Circuit and Court of Federal Claims precedent (Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000)). While the performer does not need exclusive rights (retaining copyrights, license rights, or a non-exclusive right to use the research results in its own business without paying royalties or obtaining client consent suffices, as confirmed in Lockheed Martin, Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, Tax Ct. No. 405-17, and four sample projects in Smith), agreements transferring all right, title, and interest or requiring the client's prior written consent to reuse the research (as in two disallowed sample projects in Smith) strip the performer of substantial rights. Crucially, as the Fifth Circuit held in United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) explicitly dictates that "incidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research". Moreover, under § 1.41-4A(d)(2), where a performing taxpayer retains no substantial rights and payments are contingent upon the success of the research, neither the performer nor the payor is entitled to claim any portion of the expenditures as QREs.

Conversely, when a taxpayer is the customer/payor hiring a non-employee contractor to perform qualified research (claiming 65% of eligible contract research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(1), or 75% for payments to a qualified research consortium under § 41(b)(3)(C) and 100% for eligible energy research under § 41(b)(3)(D)), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2) mandates that an expense is paid or incurred for the performance of qualified research only to the extent paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement that: (i) is entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research; (ii) provides that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer (which § 1.41-2(e)(3) defines as the taxpayer having a right—exclusive or non-exclusive—to the research results); and (iii) requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful. If an expense is paid or incurred pursuant to an agreement under which the payor's payment to the contractor is contingent on the success of the research, 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) deems the payment to be for the purchase of a finished product or result rather than the performance of research, disqualifying that payment as a contract research expense to the payor. Consequently, during an R&D examination, IRS auditors routinely issue IDRs demanding master service agreements, statements of work (SOWs), purchase orders, milestone payment schedules, intellectual property assignment and licensing clauses, termination provisions, and warranty terms to test both sides of the risk-and-rights mirror.
Comprehensive Analysis of Quantitative, Behavioral, and Technical R&D Audit Triggers

R&D tax credit audits are primarily triggered when a taxpayer's return exhibits quantifiable statistical outliers, high-scrutiny procedural behaviors, industry classification mismatches, or the inclusion of statutorily excluded activities.
Quantitative Disproportionality and Statistical Anomalies

Within the IRS's automated screening environment, quantitative disproportionality is the single most common statistical trigger. Operational audit selection models studied by IRS Research, Applied Analytics, and Statistics (RAAS) in Publication 1500 combine a return's DIF score (and its non-linear square term) with return-level variables including wages, taxable income, flow-through income, and multi-year consistency indicators. Quantitative anomalies manifest in three primary ways.

First, claiming an exceptionally large R&D credit relative to reported gross receipts, taxable income, or total company payroll signals aggressive cost allocation that deviates from peer statistical norms derived from National Research Program (NRP) baselines. While exact IRS DIF mathematical formulas and industry cutoffs are strictly confidential under IRM 4.1.2, primary Treasury/IRS Statistics of Income (SOI) data show that wages and salaries constitute approximately 69% of all reported QREs nationwide (followed by contract research at 16% and supplies at 15%), making aggressive high-percentage wage allocations the primary focus of IRS examiners: in Moore v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-20, the taxpayer's attempt to allocate 65% of its COO's compensation to QREs without task-level substantiation resulted in complete disallowance of those wages. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B), only if "substantially all" (80% or more) of an individual employee's services during the taxable year consist of qualified services may 100% of that employee's wages be claimed; claiming high percentages near or at that threshold without granular time tracking immediately attracts examiner scrutiny.

Second, significant unexplained fluctuations in claimed QREs compared to prior tax years—or relative to the three-year rolling base period under the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4), used for 69% of corporate QREs nationwide) or the fixed-base percentage period (1984–1988 or start-up rules capped at 16%) and prior four-year average annual gross receipts (subject to the 50% minimum base amount under § 41(c)(2)) under the Regular Credit method (26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1)–(3), used for 31% of corporate QREs)—flag a return for human classification review. In practice, IRS examiners are explicitly instructed by the RCCATG to examine "Consistency and Base Period Issues" under the statutory consistency rule of I.R.C. § 41(c)(5)(A) (formerly codified at I.R.C. § 41(c)(6) as cited in the 2008 RCCATG), which mandates that QREs taken into account in computing the base period must be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs for the credit year, regardless of whether the statute of limitations has expired for those base-period years.

Third, discrepancies between the QREs reported on Form 6765 and the financial figures reported elsewhere on the tax return (such as Form W-2 box 1 taxable wage totals under I.R.C. § 3401(a), Schedule C or Form 1120 salary and supply deductions, Form 1099-NEC contractor payments, or financial statement R&D disclosures) act as immediate classification triggers. For example, in a 2025 state and federal R&D audit decision published in the Indiana Register (20250430-IR-045250179NRA, April 30, 2025), examiners disallowed all claimed R&D credits after finding that the taxpayers reported "no research and development expenses either for book or for tax reporting purposes" on their underlying financial records while submitting a consultant-prepared credit study.
Behavioral and Procedural Triggers: Amended Returns, Form 6765 Section G, and Post-NOL Utilization
How and when a taxpayer claims the R&D credit carries as much weight in audit selection as the dollar magnitude of the claim.
Amended Tax Returns and Refund Claims (100% IRS Validity Screening)

According to FAQ 3 of the IRS's official Research Credit Claims (Section 41) on Amended Returns Frequently Asked Questions (updated October 1, 2026), the IRS reviews every single Research Credit claim for refund on an amended return to determine whether it is valid.

Following Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F and IRS News Release IR-2021-203, for refund claims postmarked on or after January 10, 2022 (FAQ 2), the IRS initially required taxpayers to provide five essential items of information at the time the refund claim was filed: (1) identify all business components to which the I.R.C. § 41 research credit claim relates for that year; (2) for each business component, identify all research activities performed; (3) identify the names of all individuals who performed each research activity; (4) identify the information each individual sought to discover; and (5) provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be reported on Form 6765).

For amended returns filed after June 18, 2024, the IRS scaled back upfront filing burdens under FAQ 21 (and updated FAQs 9 and 10) by waiving the requirement to submit Item 3 (individual names) and Item 4 (information each individual sought to discover) at the initial time the amended return is filed. Consequently, taxpayers filing an amended R&D refund claim after June 18, 2024 must provide three mandatory items upfront at the time of filing:

items: Business Component Identification: Identification of all business components to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that claim year (mapped by business component name/number and I.R.C. § 41(d)(2)(B) category such as Product, Process, Computer Software, Technique, Formula, or Invention per FAQ 20).
Research Activities Performed: Identification and description of all research activities performed for each business component.

Total Claim-Year QREs by Category: Total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be reported on Form 6765).

Furthermore, the IRS extended its administrative transition period twice, running through January 10, 2027. During this transition window (where the IRS aims to make validity determinations within 6 months of receipt per FAQ 5), campus employees—or field examiners for taxpayers already under audit—review claims in coordination with subject-matter experts and Division Counsel (FAQ 6). If a refund claim lacks the required upfront specificity—or merely repeats boilerplate statutory or regulatory definitions without taxpayer-specific facts (FAQ 7)—the IRS issues Letter 6426C or Letter 6428, granting the taxpayer 45 days from the letter date to "perfect" the claim (FAQs 4, 7, 8). Under FAQs 9 and 12, initial and perfecting submissions are accepted only on paper or via facsimile (fax) (with faxing to the number on the letter designated as the preferred method), and portable electronic storage devices (such as USB flash drives) are strictly rejected. If a taxpayer fails to perfect within the 45-day window, the entire claim for refund is rejected as deficient (FAQ 4), and under FAQ 15, claims rejected as deficient or non-processible are not eligible for review by the IRS Independent Office of Appeals (unlike claims disallowed solely on timeliness grounds).

Per the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, updated February 6, 2026) and FAQ 17, taxpayers filing amended returns also face three strict statutory and administrative rules. First, the I.R.C. § 280C(c)(3) reduced credit election (made at Item A on Form 6765, which reduces the gross research credit by the maximum corporate tax rate of 21%—bringing the 20% Regular Credit rate to 15.8% and the 14% ASC rate to 11.06%—to avoid reducing deductible/amortizable domestic R&E expenses by the credit amount as restored by P.L. 119-21) must be made on an original, timely filed return (including extensions) and cannot be made or revoked on an amended return. Second, the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) election (Section B of Form 6765) can be made on an amended return only if the taxpayer had not previously claimed the research credit on an original return or a prior amended return for that tax year, and no extension of time to make the ASC election will be granted. Third, while the upfront specificity items apply to both formal and informal refund claims, Form 1120 corporate taxpayers are strictly prohibited from filing "informal" research credit refund claims and must file a formal amended return pursuant to Notice 2008-39 (FAQ 17).
Upfront Disclosure on Original Returns: Form 6765 Section G (Mandatory Post-2025)

The updated form structures the research credit around three core inquiries—What did you make?, Why is it qualified?, and How much did it cost?—by introducing Section G (Business Component Information).

Under the official Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), Section G is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026, and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025, unless the taxpayer satisfies one of two statutory exemptions. Under the first exemption (Qualified Small Business [QSB] Payroll Tax Credit Exemption), Section G is not required if the taxpayer is a qualified small business as defined under I.R.C. § 41(h)(3) and checks the box on Form 6765 to elect a reduced payroll tax credit (up to $500,000 per year for tax years beginning after December 31, 2022 under § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(II), which must be elected on or before the due date of the originally filed income tax return including extensions, is disallowed if elected in 5 or more preceding tax years, and is claimed via Form 8974 on the employment tax return for the first quarter beginning after the income tax return is filed to reduce the employer share of Social Security tax by up to $250,000 per quarter and then the employer share of Medicare tax). Under the second exemption ($1.5M QREs and $50M Gross Receipts Exception), Section G is not required if the taxpayer has total QREs determined at the controlled-group level on Line 48 equal to or less than $1.5 million, has average annual gross receipts for the prior 3 tax years equal to or less than $50 million (determined under I.R.C. § 448(c)(3), without regard to subparagraph § 448(c)(3)(A)), and is reporting the research credit on an original return.

Taxpayers required to complete Section G must follow the "80%/Top 50" reporting rule determined at the controlled-group level: the filer must report itemized information in descending order of total QREs per business component for at least 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components. Any remaining business components beyond the 80%/Top 50 threshold are reported on a single line by entering "Aggregate Business Components" in Column 49(c) and entering the aggregate QRE dollar amounts in Columns 50 through 56 (leaving all other Section G columns blank). For each itemized business component in the 80%/Top 50, Section G requires reporting the controlled-group entity's Employer Identification Number (EIN) in Column 49(a), the entity's Principal Business Activity (PBA) code in Column 49(b), the business component's name or unique alphanumeric identifier matching books and records in Column 49(c), and the component type ("Product", "Process", or "All Others") in Column 49(d). If the business component is software, Column 49(e) requires selecting its specific regulatory classification under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(E): (A) IUS (Internal Use Software); (B) DFS (Dual Function Software: [1] where no third-party subset is identified and the DFS safe harbor is not applied, [2] where a third-party subset is identified and the remaining dual-function subset is subject to the High Threshold of Innovation [HTI] test, or [3] with the 25% DFS safe harbor applied); or (C) Excepted from IUS treatment ([1] software developed for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research, [2] software developed for internal use in a production process meeting § 41(d)(1), or [3] a new or improved integrated package of software and hardware). Columns 50 through 56 then capture the quantitative QRE breakdown per business component across qualified wages, supply expenses (Column 54, feeding into Section F Line 43), rental/lease costs of computers used in qualified research (Column 55, feeding into Section F Line 44), and eligible contract research expenses (Column 56, feeding into Section F Line 45). Taxpayers using Rev. Proc. 2011-42 statistical sampling must still report the 80%/Top 50 components, append "sample" to sampled component identifiers, and attach Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf.
Post-NOL Credit Utilization

Beginning to utilize accumulated R&D tax credit carryforwards immediately after extended periods of generating Net Operating Losses (NOLs) is a recognized behavioral audit trigger. When a company transitions from a multi-year loss position into tax profitability and applies banked research credit carryforwards to offset current federal income tax liability, IRS screening models flag the sudden reduction in cash tax payments, prompting examiners to inspect both the utilization year and the credit generation years to verify whether the underlying QREs were properly substantiated when originally incurred (which is why tax practitioners advise retaining full R&D credit substantiation files until the limitation period for the final carryforward utilization year closes).
Industry Profile, NAICS/PBA Codes, and Cascading Return Red Flags

Industry classification shapes R&D audit probability from two opposite directions: high-concentration R&D sectors face specialized technical scrutiny over the boundary between routine commercial operations and true experimentation, while low-R&D service sectors trigger immediate algorithmic anomaly flags when Form 6765 is attached.
Manufacturing's Share of R&D Claims and Sector Audit Rates

By contrast, authoritative federal tax return data compiled by the U.S. Department of the Treasury Office of Tax Analysis from IRS Statistics of Income (SOI) Corporation Research Credit tables (Form 6765) demonstrate an even higher concentration in manufacturing—particularly by dollar volume. In the Treasury Office of Tax Analysis study of 15,873 corporate tax returns claiming $10.8 billion in current-year research credits (representing 93% of the $11.6 billion in current-year research credits claimed across all corporate and individual returns combined), 6,219 corporate manufacturers claimed nearly $6.6 billion in research credits—accounting for 39% of all corporate returns claiming the credit and 61% of total corporate research credit dollars. Furthermore, Treasury's SOI data highlight extreme size concentration across corporate claimants: large corporations with gross receipts of $250 million or more represented 14% of corporate tax filers claiming the credit but generated 84% of total corporate credit dollars, whereas small and mid-size corporations with gross receipts under $50 million accounted for just over 72% of corporate returns claiming the credit but generated less than 11% of total credit dollars (with corporations under $5 million in gross receipts accounting for 42% of claimant returns and less than 6% of credit dollars). Under the hierarchy of evidentiary authority, the U.S. Treasury / IRS SOI data carry primary authoritative weight for U.S. corporate tax returns, whereas the MGO CPA percentages represent a secondary consultancy estimate across entity types.

NAICS / Principal Business Activity (PBA) Code Screening

Conversely, claiming the R&D tax credit under a North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) or Principal Business Activity (PBA) code associated with retail, personal services, or hospitality invites immediate algorithmic anomaly review. The IRS systematically tracks industry codes on R&D filings: Column 49(b) of Section G on Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) explicitly requires the filer to enter the Principal Business Activity (PBA) code for the entity conducting research on each reported business component.
Cascading General Tax Return Red Flags

An R&D tax credit examination does not have to be triggered by Form 6765 alone; general compliance red flags elsewhere on a federal tax return can trigger a broad income tax audit that cascades into a technical review of the R&D credit. General audit triggers documented in tax practice commentary (Kiplinger, What Are Your Chances of an IRS Audit? 18 Audit Red Flags, updated January 6, 2026) include reporting substantial or multi-year Schedule C business losses—especially by sole proprietors reporting at least $100,000 in gross receipts or using business losses to offset Form W-2 wages or investment income. Under the hobby-loss safe harbor presumption of I.R.C. § 183, if an activity shows a profit in at least 3 out of 5 consecutive tax years (or 2 out of 7 years for horse breeding), the law presumes the taxpayer is engaged in a valid business for profit; failing that safe harbor requires the taxpayer to prove a genuine profit motive under the facts-and-circumstances test. Similarly, claiming 100% business use of a vehicle—particularly heavy SUVs or large trucks purchased late in the tax year that qualify for favorable depreciation and expensing write-offs when no other vehicle is available for personal use—or claiming disproportionately large rental losses, bad-debt deductions, or worthless-stock write-offs spikes return-level DIF scores. Under IRM 4.22.2 (NRP Case Building) and standard examination procedures, once a tax return is assigned to a revenue agent for any reason, the examiner conducts a comprehensive pre-contact review of all material items on the return, making an attached Form 6765 a prime target for expansion of the audit scope.
Technical Ineligibility: Statutory Exclusions Under I.R.C. § 41(d)(3)–(4)

To constitute statutory "qualified research" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2), an activity must satisfy all four prongs of the Four-Part Test applied separately to each discrete business component under § 41(d)(2)(A):

items: The Section 174 / 174A Tax-Deductibility & Uncertainty Test (§ 41(d)(1)(A) & 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(2)(i), (a)(3)(i)): The research must be research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified domestic research or experimental expenditures under I.R.C. § 174 / § 174A—meaning costs incurred in the taxpayer's trade or business intended to eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving a business component. (Legislative Note: While the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act [TCJA, P.L. 115-97] required 5-year amortization for domestic R&E expenditures and 15-year amortization for foreign R&E expenditures for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, the 2025 Reconciliation Act [P.L. 119-21, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act / OBBBA, analyzed in Congressional Research Service Report R48631, August 14, 2025] permanently restored 100% immediate domestic R&E expensing under I.R.C. § 174A and restored the research credit basis adjustment for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, shifting the Marginal Effective Tax Rate [METR] on debt-financed R&D in 2025 from -113.6% to -154.8% for corporations and from -9.3% to -318.6% for noncorporate businesses.)

The Technological in Nature Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i) & 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(4)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature—meaning the process of experimentation used to discover the information fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii)–(iii), the taxpayer need not seek information that exceeds or expands the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the field, nor must the research succeed, and the issuance of a utility patent under 35 U.S.C. § 151 (other than a design patent under 35 U.S.C. § 171) serves as conclusive evidence that this discovery requirement is met (the "patent safe harbor").

The Permitted / Qualified Purpose Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii), § 41(d)(3)(A), & 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii)): The application of the discovered information must be intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

The Process of Experimentation Test (§ 41(d)(1)(C) & 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)–(6)): Substantially all (80% or more) of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation—an evaluative process (involving the identification of uncertainty, identification of one or more alternatives to eliminate that uncertainty, and conduct of an evaluation through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology) capable of evaluating alternatives where capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain at the outset. Under the "shrinking-back rule" of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(b)(2), if the overall business component fails the Four-Part Test (for example, failing the 80% threshold), the requirements are applied iteratively to the next most significant subset of elements of the product or process until either a qualifying subcomponent is reached or the most basic element fails.

items: Style, Taste, Cosmetic, or Seasonal Design Factors (§ 41(d)(3)(B) & 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii)): Research relating to style, taste, cosmetic appearance, or seasonal design factors is never treated as conducted for a qualified purpose.

Research After Commercial Production (§ 41(d)(4)(A) & 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(2)): Any research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component—defined as when the component is developed to the point where it is ready for commercial sale or use, or meets the basic functional and economic requirements of the taxpayer for its sale or use, whichever occurs earlier—is excluded. Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii) and the IRS Aerospace Industry Audit Techniques Guide, activities deemed to occur after commercial production include preproduction planning for a finished business component, tooling-up for production (acquiring or manufacturing special production-rate tooling), trial production runs, and troubleshooting or debugging to detect faults in existing production equipment or processes. (Statutory Exception: Under the special rule of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) and Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component from the product being manufactured; thus, experimental development of a new manufacturing process can qualify independently even after the underlying product design is finalized.)

Adaptation of Existing Business Components (§ 41(d)(4)(B)): Any research related to the customization or adaptation of an existing business component to meet a particular customer's requirement or need is excluded.

Duplication of Existing Business Components (§ 41(d)(4)(C)): Any research related to the reproduction of an existing business component (in whole or in part) from a physical examination of the business component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information—including reverse engineering—is excluded.

Surveys, Management Functions, Market Research, and Routine Quality Control (§ 41(d)(4)(D)(i)–(v)): The statute explicitly excludes any (i) efficiency survey, (ii) activity relating to management function or technique, (iii) market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), (iv) routine data collection, or (v) routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control.

Internal-Use Computer Software (§ 41(d)(4)(E)): Except to the extent provided in regulations, any research with respect to computer software which is developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use by the taxpayer is excluded, unless the software is developed for use in an activity which constitutes qualified research (§ 41(d)(4)(E)(i)), a production process which meets the requirements of § 41(d)(1) (§ 41(d)(4)(E)(ii)), an integrated hardware-software package, or satisfies the regulatory three-part High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test (or the 25% Dual Function Software [DFS] safe harbor) reported in Column 49(e) of Form 6765 Section G.

Foreign Research (§ 41(d)(4)(F)): Any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States is excluded, regardless of whether the employees or contractors are paid by a U.S. taxpayer.

Social Sciences, Arts, or Humanities (§ 41(d)(4)(G)): Any research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities (including economics, business management, behavioral studies, or historical/literary research) is excluded.

Funded Research (§ 41(d)(4)(H), 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d), & 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)): Any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity) where the performing taxpayer fails the financial risk or substantial rights standards of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(2).

items: Hourly Consulting / Time Billing Approach: Standard hourly rates ranging from $195 to $395 per hour based on the specific professional assigned and total hours expended for advisory services, claim preparation, IDR responses, or audit representation (with no charge for routine out-of-pocket disbursements unless an unforeseen, substantial expense is agreed upon in advance).

Fixed-Fee Engagement: A flat, pre-agreed fee quote determined during a preliminary complimentary scoping discussion based on estimated hours, technical complexity, and project scope, covering technical interviews, financial QRE tracing, and final audit-ready report generation.

Phased / Hybrid Milestone Model: A structured model combining hourly and fixed-fee elements broken down by discrete project milestones (scoping, technical write-up, and financial QRE calculation) to manage cash flow across multi-year or multi-jurisdictional claims.

body.text: While a capped flat fee with a "no-benefit, no-fee" floor does not incentivize inflating a claim above the fixed fee threshold in the manner that an uncapped percentage-of-credit fee does, a fee conditioned on obtaining a tax benefit is still technically classified as a contingent fee under Treasury Department Circular 230.

Primary regulatory, judicial, and IRS enforcement records explain why advisor fee structures matter directly for R&D audit triggers. In September 2007, to prevent practitioners from exploiting the audit selection process, the Treasury Department promulgated T.D. 9359 (72 FR 54540, amending 31 C.F.R. § 10.27 of Circular 230, clarified by Notice 2008-43), which broadly prohibited practitioners from charging contingent fees for any matter before the IRS—including preparing or filing original returns, amended returns, and claims for refund or credit—permitting contingent fees only in narrow exceptions (such as an IRS examination or challenge to an original return, an amended return filed within 120 days of an examination notice, claims solely concerning statutory interest or penalties, whistleblower claims under I.R.C. § 7623, or judicial proceedings). However, in Gerald Lee Ridgely, Jr. v. Jacob J. Lew, et al., 55 F. Supp. 3d 89, Civil Action No. 1:12-cv-00565 (CRC) (D.D.C. July 16, 2014) (relying on Loving v. IRS, 742 F.3d 1013 (D.C. Cir. 2014)), the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia held that the IRS lacked statutory authority under 31 U.S.C. § 330(a)(1) to regulate fee arrangements prior to adversarial representation (before a practitioner submits a power-of-attorney form) and issued a permanent injunction invalidating 31 C.F.R. § 10.27 to the extent it banned CPAs and practitioners from charging contingent fees for preparing and filing "Ordinary Refund Claims". (Note: On December 26, 2024, Treasury published proposed regulations in the Federal Register, Vol. 89, No. 247, Doc. 2024-29371, proposing to classify certain contingent fee arrangements as disreputable conduct aligned with professional accounting standards.)

Because Ridgely v. Lew legally permitted boutique R&D providers to charge percentage-based contingency fees on refund claims, the IRS directly incorporated contingency fee arrangements into its audit risk screening criteria. In Tier I Research Credit Claims Issue Directive #2 (LMSB-4-0608-035), the IRS explicitly stated that its Mandatory Research Credit Claim IDR was created to identify marketed tax studies that "lack adequate documentation, use high-level estimates based on invalid assumptions, lack nexus between qualified research expenses (QREs) and business components, or are prepared on a contingency fee basis". Similarly, Chapter II of the IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (LMSB-04-0508-030) lists "The RC Claim Engagement Letter" as a primary examination tool, instructing IRS auditors to demand the consultant's engagement letter in the initial IDR to inspect the fee terms and scope of work. Engaging an R&D advisor on a strict hourly or non-contingent fixed fee therefore eliminates a documented IRS audit flag at the outset of an examination.
Hypothetical Worked Example: Quantitative Disproportionality and I.R.C. § 6676 Penalty Exposure

Suppose Apex Cloud Systems, Inc. (a hypothetical U.S. C corporation filing an amended return for a prior tax year) has $10,000,000 in annual gross receipts and employs 20 software developers earning $2,000,000 in total Form W-2 box 1 taxable wages under I.R.C. § 3401(a). In addition, Apex paid $400,000 to an outside domestic software contractor to perform post-commercial-production bug maintenance and customer-specific interface adaptations under a contract where the contractor retained exclusive intellectual property rights. Assume Apex had $500,000 in average annual QREs over the three preceding tax years and calculates its credit using the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A), which equals 14% of current-year QREs exceeding 50% of average QREs for the 3 preceding taxable years. With prior 3-year average QREs of $500,000, the statutory ASC base (50% of the prior 3-year average under § 41(c)(4)(A)) equals 0.50 × $500,000 = $250,000.

In Scenario A (Aggressive Contingency-Fee Claim), relying on generalized oral recollections without project time logs, an aggressive contingency-fee advisor allocates 80% of total developer wages to QREs, yielding $2,000,000 × 0.80 = $1,600,000 in wage QREs. Failing to screen out post-production debugging (§ 41(d)(4)(A)), customer adaptation (§ 41(d)(4)(B)), and lack of rights (§ 1.41-2(e)(3)), the advisor also includes the $400,000 contractor spend at the statutory 65% contract research rate under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) and 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-2(e)(1), adding $400,000 × 0.65 = $260,000 in contract QREs. Total Aggressive QREs equal $1,600,000 + $260,000 = $1,860,000 (representing a 272% spike over the $500,000 three-year historical average—a severe statistical variance trigger). Subtracting the $250,000 ASC base leaves $1,610,000 in excess QREs, generating an initial Aggressive ASC Refund Claim of $1,610,000 × 0.14 = $225,400.

In Scenario B (Conservative Fixed-Fee Claim), using contemporaneous project-tracking records and engineering interviews that separate new algorithm experimentation from routine maintenance and management meetings (as required by Little Sandy Coal and Moore), a conservative fixed-fee advisor substantiates 30% of developer wages across qualifying business components, yielding $2,000,000 × 0.30 = $600,000 in wage QREs. Applying proactive statutory screening, the advisor excludes 100% of the $400,000 post-production/adapted contractor spend ($0 in contract QREs), resulting in Total Conservative QREs of $600,000 (a defensible 20% increase over the $500,000 three-year average). Subtracting the $250,000 ASC base leaves $350,000 in excess QREs, generating a Conservative ASC Refund Claim of $350,000 × 0.14 = $49,000.

Upon mandatory amended-return review and substantive examination of Scenario A, the IRS disallows the unsubstantiated 50% wage overstatement ($1,000,000 in wages) and the ineligible $260,000 contract research claim, reducing allowable QREs from $1,860,000 to $600,000 and allowable credits from $225,400 to $49,000. Under I.R.C. § 6676(b), the disallowed "excessive amount" is $225,400 − $49,000 = $176,400. Assessing the mandatory 20% erroneous refund claim penalty under I.R.C. § 6676(a) on the excessive amount lacking a reasonable basis yields a statutory penalty of $176,400 × 0.20 = $35,280. Deducting the $35,280 penalty from the $49,000 allowable credit leaves a net retained tax benefit of $13,720 (before accounting for internal executive time and external legal/accounting defense costs)—representing a 72% reduction in net tax benefit compared to claiming the conservative, fully substantiated $49,000 credit from the outset:

body.text: Synthesis and Expert Conclusion
What Triggers an R&D Tax Credit Audit

R&D tax credit audits are primarily initiated by statistical screening algorithms—specifically the IRS's Discriminant Function (DIF) system for corporate returns with total assets under $10 million (Activity Codes 203–217) and automatic LB&I Ogden Campus classification routing for corporate returns with total assets of $10 million or more (Activity Codes 219–230)—combined with random compliance sampling under the National Research Program (NRP) and targeted procedural filters. While filing Form 6765 on an original return is not an automatic audit trigger, audit probability rises sharply when a claim exhibits quantitative disproportionality (excessive QRE-to-wage or credit-to-revenue ratios, abrupt year-over-year spending spikes, base-period inconsistencies violating I.R.C. § 41(c)(5), or mismatches with general ledger and Form W-2 records), when a taxpayer files in a high-scrutiny sector such as manufacturing (which accounts for 39% of corporate claimant returns and 61% of corporate credit dollars per U.S. Treasury/IRS SOI data, and a 16.84% sector audit rate in the 2026 Boast.ai benchmark) or under an incongruous Principal Business Activity (PBA/NAICS) code, or when general return red flags (such as Schedule C hobby losses under I.R.C. § 183 or 100% business vehicle deductions) trigger an examination that cascades into the research credit. Above all, filing an amended return to claim an R&D refund guarantees upfront IRS scrutiny: under current IRS procedures (with transition rules extended through January 10, 2027), the IRS screens 100% of amended R&D refund claims for specificity under 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) prior to audit initiation—a gatekeeping regime established by Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F after the Ninth Circuit held in Harper v. United States (2021) that conducting a substantive audit waives the government's specificity defense.
How Conservative Filing Lowers Audit Risk: Strategic and Quantitative Mitigation

A conservative filing methodology lowers audit risk by neutralizing the quantitative and behavioral anomalies that statistical screening models and IRS classifiers target. By engaging on hourly ($195–$395/hour) or fixed-fee structures rather than percentage-of-credit contingency fees, a conservative practice removes the financial conflict of interest that drives aggressive advisors to inflate employee time allocations or bundle routine operational costs into QREs—and directly avoids the contingency-fee risk factor targeted by the IRS's Mandatory IDR and RCCATG guidelines. Simultaneously, proactively excluding activities barred by I.R.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and § 41(d)(4)(A)–(H) (such as post-production tooling and troubleshooting, customer adaptations, reverse engineering, management functions, market research, foreign research, social sciences, and funded contract work lacking financial risk or substantial rights under 26 C.F.R. §§ 1.41-2(e) and 1.41-4A(d) as enforced in Grigsby and Smith) keeps claimed QREs within established industry norms, protects the 80% "substantially all" experimentation threshold enforced in Little Sandy Coal, and insulates the taxpayer from the 20% erroneous refund claim penalty under I.R.C. § 6676(a).
How Conservative Filing Lowers Audit Risk: Structural and Procedural Mitigation

Once a return is screened at intake or selected for examination, structural quality controls determine whether the credit is sustained. Integrating an ISO 31000-aligned risk management workflow (noting that ISO 31000:2018 superseded ISO 31000:2009) with an ISO 27001 information security framework standardizes contemporaneous data collection and project-level cost accounting from the start of the engagement. Subjecting every claim to a mandatory multi-disciplinary Six-Eye Review—combining independent engineering/scientific verification of the Four-Part Test with CPA or Enrolled Agent verification of financial tracing and tax law compliance—ensures that the resulting documentation package satisfies both the upfront business-component disclosure mandates of 26 C.F.R. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) and Form 6765 Section G (mandatory for non-exempt original returns for tax years beginning after 2025) and the substantive recordkeeping and project-to-expense nexus standards of 26 C.F.R. § 1.41-4(d).
